description:
Somos un equipo joven, ambicioso y emprendedor con una idea clara: convertir la innovación en soluciones reales.

En este Space Apps afrontamos el reto Flame in Freefall, centrado en la seguridad contra incendios en el espacio.

Trabajamos rápido, pensamos en grande y apostamos por proyectos con impacto real, en el espacio y en la Tierra.
summary: JAPAX turns three decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into clear answers about how fire behaves, and how to stop it, in the places astronauts will live. We catalogued 19 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive, with their DOIs, hardware and file inventories, and we compute every statistic directly from the real experimental tables (FLEX: 274 droplet tests; BASS-II: 129 solid-fuel tests). The Simulator lets anyone touch a 3D NASA model (spacesuit, ISS, lunar module) and see how a fire could pass from component to component, with suppression measures and a downloadable report. An assistant, Pax, explains results in plain language, and every number is checked against cited evidence. Because PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data, lunar and Martian conditions are shown honestly as gaps, never extrapolated. Fire is the most dangerous accident on a spacecraft; JaPax makes that science understandable to everyone.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

JAPAX ("Flame in Freefall" challenge) is a web application that converts NASA's microgravity combustion research into answers a non-specialist can use: what burns, how fast a flame spreads, what stops it, and what we still do not know. It is organised around saving lives: fire is one of the most dangerous events on a spacecraft (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) and future Moon habitats will use atmospheres and materials that change how things burn.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data layer. We read the public NASA PSI API at build time and catalogue 19 combustion investigations (BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, ACME, SAFFIRE, SAME and others) with PSI ID, DOI, hypotheses, hardware, publications and file inventories. The experimental tables of FLEX (PSI-69, 274 droplet tests) and BASS-II (PSI-25, 129 solid-fuel tests) are processed in the browser: every count and percentage is computed from the recorded rows, with no modelling.

2. Simulator (/simulator). A WebGL (three.js) scene shows the molecular-level flame and real NASA 3D models (EMU spacesuit, ISS, Apollo Lunar Module). Touching a component identifies it and runs a component-to-component fire-spread graph (a qualitative model), lets the user apply suppression measures, warns before a rupture, and produces a results window with CSV and text export. Every fact in the component catalogues carries a source tag; anything without a source is flagged "estimated" and gaps are listed explicitly.

3. Evidence tabs. Measured spread rates (SAFFIRE), suppression evidence (CO2 and helium, FLEX), the effect of pressure and oxygen (BASS/BASS-II) and the lunar anchors (LUCI 2025, planned FM2) are shown with their NASA source.

4. Pax assistant. Answers are structured: numbers are computed by our own code from the evidence; a Claude model can only narrate, and a guard removes any figure not supported by the evidence.

5. Dashboard, Explorer, History (31 events), Glossary, Methodology and References pages document the data, the relevance score (an editorial 0-100 prioritisation aid, not a NASA metric) and every limitation.

SCIENTIFIC HONESTY (what makes it valid)

- Each value is labelled measured / predicted / estimated, with PSI ID, DOI or NTRS report.

- PSI contains no partial-gravity combustion data. Lunar and Martian cases are shown as gaps and are not extrapolated; the single lunar-gravity anchor is LUCI (NTRS 20250010653), and FM2 is planned to fly in late 2026.

- The "about 12.7 TB" figure is the total size NASA declares for the 19 investigations (decimal terabytes), not data processed by JaPax; the API enumerates only part of it file by file. This is stated on the References page.

- The two experimental tables were obtained from a public CC0 copy because the PSI download service was unavailable; their byte sizes match NASA's metadata (24,776 and 16,590).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Teachers, students, researchers and mission planners get one place where decades of NASA fire-safety data are searchable, comparable and explained, with the open questions made visible. It helps prioritise which materials and atmospheres deserve testing for lunar habitats, and it communicates why spacecraft fire safety matters to the general public.

TOOLS

Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, three.js 0.187 (WebGL), custom SVG charts, Anthropic Claude (claude-sonnet-5-5) via the Anthropic TypeScript SDK for optional narration, NASA PSI and NTRS public APIs, Vercel hosting. A 90-test automated suite (node --test) validates the component engine, catalogues, CSV export and run records. The interface is bilingual (English default, Spanish).

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a static dashboard, users touch a real NASA 3D model and watch a fire's path through its components, then see the measured evidence behind it. The assistant is deliberately constrained so it cannot invent numbers, and uncertainty is a visible feature, not a footnote.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility (skip link, keyboard use, mobile layout, plain-language explanations), scientific traceability (a citation for every number), honesty about gaps, performance on ordinary laptops (automatic 2D fallback if WebGL is missing), and licensing (NASA media guidelines for 3D models, open-source licences for libraries; all graphics are original SVG; no copyrighted music or images).
